entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8020"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen12440" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1-Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:1-22</reference>.<div eID="gen12440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12441" type="x-p"/> Earthly pursuits are no doubt lawful in their proper time and order (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1-Eccl.3.8">Ec 3:1-8</reference>), but unprofitable when out of time and place; as for instance, when pursued as the solid and chief good (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.9">Ec 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.10">10</reference>); whereas God makes everything beautiful in its season, which man obscurely comprehends (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>). God allows man to enjoy moderately and virtuously His earthly gifts (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">13</reference>). What consoles us amidst the instability of earthly blessings is, God's counsels are immutable (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Ec 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8020"/>1. Man has his appointed cycle of seasons and vicissitudes, as the sun, wind, and water (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.5-Eccl.1.7">Ec 1:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen12442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purpose--</hi>as there is a fixed "season" in God's "purposes" (for example, He has fixed the "time" when man is "to be born," and "to die," <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.2">Ec 3:2</reference>), so there is a lawful "time" for man to carry out his "purposes" and inclinations. God does not condemn, but approves of, the use of earthly blessings (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>); it is the abuse that He condemns, the making them the chief end (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.31">1Co 7:31</reference>). The earth, without human desires, love, taste, joy, sorrow, would be a dreary waste, without water; but, on the other hand, the misplacing and excess of them, as of a flood, need control. Reason and revelation are given to control them. <div eID="gen12443" type="x-p"/>

God allows man to enjoy moderately and virtuously His earthly gifts ( Ec 3:12 , 13 ). What consoles us amidst the instability of earthly blessings is, God's counsels are immutable ( Ec 3:14 ). 1. The earth, without human desires, love, taste, joy, sorrow, would be a dreary waste, without water; but, on the other hand, the misplacing and excess of them, as of a flood, need control. Reason and revelation are given to control them.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8021"/><div sID="gen12444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8021"/><hi type="bold">2. time to die--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.31.15">Psa 31:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.27">He 9:27</reference>).<div eID="gen12444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plant--</hi>A man can no more reverse the times and order of "planting," and of "digging up," and transplanting, than he can alter the times fixed for his "birth" and "death." To try to "plant" out of season is vanity, however good in season; so to make earthly things the chief end is vanity, however good they be in order and season. Gill takes it, not so well, figuratively (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.7">Jr 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">Am 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.15.13">Mt 15:13</reference>). <div eID="gen12445" type="x-p"/>

To try to "plant" out of season is vanity, however good in season; so to make earthly things the chief end is vanity, however good they be in order and season. Gill takes it, not so well, figuratively ( Jr 18:7 , 9 ; Am 9:15 ; Mt 15:13 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8028"/><div sID="gen12463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8028"/>9. But these earthly pursuits, while lawful in their season, are "unprofitable" when made by man, what God never intended them to be, the chief good. Solomon had tried to create an artificial forced joy, at times when he ought rather to have been serious; the result, therefore, of his labor to be happy, out of God's order, was disappointment. "A time to plant" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.2">Ec 3:2</reference>) refers to his planting (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.5">Ec 2:5</reference>); "laugh" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.4">Ec 3:4</reference>), to <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1">Ec 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>; "his mirth," "laughter"; "build up," "gather stones" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.3">Ec 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.5">5</reference>), to his "building" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.4">Ec 2:4</reference>); "embrace," "love," to his "princess" (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.8">Ec 2:8</reference>); "get" (perhaps also "gather," <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.5">Ec 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.6">6</reference>), to his "gathering" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.8">Ec 2:8</reference>). All these were of "no profit," because not in God's time and order of bestowing happiness. <div eID="gen12463" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. But these earthly pursuits, while lawful in their season, are "unprofitable" when made by man, what God never intended them to be, the chief good. Solomon had tried to create an artificial forced joy, at times when he ought rather to have been serious; the result, therefore, of his labor to be happy, out of God's order, was disappointment. "A time to plant" ( Ec 3:2 ) refers to his planting ( Ec 2:5 ); "laugh" ( Ec 3:4 ), to Ec 2:1 , 2 ; "his mirth," "laughter"; "build up," "gather stones" ( Ec 3:3 , 5 ), to his "building" ( Ec 2:4 ); "embrace," "love," to his "princess" (see on Ec 2:8 ); "get" (perhaps also "gather," Ec 3:5 , 6 ), to his "gathering" ( Ec 2:8 ). All these were of "no profit," because not in God's time and order of bestowing happiness.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8030"/><div sID="gen12465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8030"/><hi type="bold">11. his time--</hi>that is, in its proper season (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>), opposed to worldlings putting earthly pursuits out of their proper time and place (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.9">Ec 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set the world in their heart--</hi>given them capacities to understand the world of nature as reflecting God's wisdom in its beautiful order and times (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.19">Ro 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). "Everything" answers to "world," in the parallelism.<div eID="gen12466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so that--</hi>that is, but in such a manner that man only sees a portion, not the whole "from beginning to end" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.4">Re 15:4</reference>). Parkhurst, for "world," translates: "Yet He hath put obscurity in the midst of them," literally, "a secret," so man's mental dimness of sight as to the full mystery of God's works. So Holden and Weiss. This incapacity for "finding out" (comprehending) God's work is chiefly the fruit of the fall. The worldling ever since, not knowing God's time and order, labors in vain, because out of time and place. <div eID="gen12467" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8031"/><div sID="gen12468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8031"/><hi type="bold">12. in them--</hi>in God's works (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>), as far as relates to man's duty. Man cannot fully comprehend them, but he ought joyfully to receive ("rejoice in") God's gifts, and "do good" with them to himself and to others. This is never out of season (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">Ga 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.10">10</reference>). Not sensual joy and self-indulgence (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.4">Php 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.16">Jas 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen12468" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 12. in them-- in God's works ( Ec 3:11 ), as far as relates to man's duty. Man cannot fully comprehend them, but he ought joyfully to receive ("rejoice in") God's gifts, and "do good" with them to himself and to others. This is never out of season ( Ga 6:9 , 10 ). Not sensual joy and self-indulgence ( Php 4:4 ; Jas 4:16 , 17 ).

(<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.12">1Sa 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.34">Psa 89:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.35">Mt 24:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen12470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>as opposed to man's perishing labors (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.15-Eccl.2.18">Ec 2:15-18</reference>).<div eID="gen12471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">any thing taken from it--</hi>opposed to man's "crooked and wanting" works (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">Ec 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.13">7:13</reference>). The event of man's labors depends wholly on God's immutable purpose. Man's part, therefore, is to do and enjoy every earthly thing in its proper season (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">13</reference>), not setting aside God's order, but observing deep reverence towards God; for the mysteriousness and unchangeableness of God's purposes are designed to lead "man to fear before Him." Man knows not the event of each act: otherwise he would think himself independent of God. <div eID="gen12472" type="x-p"/>

Resumption of <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ec 1:9</reference>. Whatever changes there be, the succession of events is ordered by God's "everlasting" laws (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Ec 3:14</reference>), and returns in a fixed cycle.<div eID="gen12473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">requireth that ... past--</hi>After many changes, God's law requires the return of the same cycle of events, as in the past, literally, "that which is driven on." The parallel clauses of the verse support English Version. <div eID="gen12474" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8035"/><div sID="gen12475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8035"/>16. Here a difficulty is suggested. If God "requires" events to move in their perpetual cycle, why are the wicked allowed to deal unrighteously in the place where injustice ought least of all to be; namely, "the place of judgment" (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jr 12:1</reference>)? <div eID="gen12475" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8036"/><div sID="gen12476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8036"/>17. Solution of it. There is a coming judgment in which God will vindicate His righteous ways. The sinner's "time" of his unrighteous "work" is short. God also has His "time" and "work" of judgment; and, meanwhile, is overruling, for good at last, what seems now dark. Man cannot now "find out" the plan of God's ways (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference>). If judgment instantly followed every sin, there would be no scope for free will, faith, and perseverance of saints in spite of difficulties. The previous darkness will make the light at last the more glorious.<div eID="gen12476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.3.17-Job.3.19">Job 3:17-19</reference>) in eternity, in the presence of the Divine Judge, opposed to the "there," in the human place of judgment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>): so "from thence" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Ge 49:24</reference>). <div eID="gen12477" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8037"/><div sID="gen12478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8037"/><hi type="bold">18. estate--</hi>The estate of fallen man is so ordered (these wrongs are permitted), that God might "manifest," that is, thereby prove them, and that they might themselves see their mortal frailty, like that of the beasts.<div eID="gen12478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sons of men--</hi>rather, "sons of Adam," a phrase used for "fallen men." The toleration of injustice until the judgment is designed to "manifest" men's characters in their fallen state, to see whether the oppressed will bear themselves aright amidst their wrongs, knowing that the time is short, and there is a coming judgment. The oppressed share in death, but the comparison to "beasts" applies especially to the ungodly oppressors (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">Psa 49:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">20</reference>). They too need to be "manifested" ("proved"), whether, considering that they must soon die as the "beasts," and fearing the judgment to come, they will repent (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Da 4:27</reference>). <div eID="gen12479" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8038"/><div sID="gen12480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8038"/>19. Literally, "For the sons of men (Adam) are a mere chance, as also the beast is a mere chance." These words can only be the sentiments of the skeptical oppressors. God's delay in judgment gives scope for the "manifestation" of their infidelity (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3">2Pe 3:3</reference>,<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">4</reference>). They are "brute beasts," morally (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.18">Ec 3:18</reference>; Jude 10); and they end by maintaining that man, physically, has no pre-eminence over the beast, both alike being "fortuities." Probably this was the language of Solomon himself in his apostasy. He answers it in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">Ec 3:21</reference>. If <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">Ec 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.20">20</reference> be his words, they express only that as regards liability to death, excluding the future judgment, as the skeptic oppressors do, man is on a level with the beast. Life is "vanity," if regarded independently of religion. But <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">Ec 3:21</reference> points out the vast difference between them in respect to the future destiny; also (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ec 3:17</reference>) beasts have no "judgment" to come.<div eID="gen12480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breath--</hi>vitality. <div eID="gen12481" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 19. Literally, "For the sons of men (Adam) are a mere chance, as also the beast is a mere chance." These words can only be the sentiments of the skeptical oppressors. God's delay in judgment gives scope for the "manifestation" of their infidelity ( Ec 8:11 ; Psa 55:19 ; 2Pe 3:3 , 4 ). They are "brute beasts," morally ( Ec 3:18 ; Jude 10); and they end by maintaining that man, physically, has no pre-eminence over the beast, both alike being "fortuities." Probably this was the language of Solomon himself in his apostasy. He answers it in Ec 3:21 . If Ec 3:19 , 20 be his words, they express only that as regards liability to death, excluding the future judgment, as the skeptic oppressors do, man is on a level with the beast. Life is "vanity," if regarded independently of religion. But Ec 3:21 points out the vast difference between them in respect to the future destiny; also ( Ec 3:17 ) beasts have no "judgment" to come. breath-- vitality.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8039"/><div sID="gen12482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8039"/><hi type="bold">21. Who knoweth--</hi>Not doubt of the destination of man's spirit (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Ec 12:7</reference>); but "how few, by reason of the outward mortality to which man is as liable as the beast and which is the ground of the skeptic's argument, comprehend the wide difference between man and the beast" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Is 53:1</reference>). The Hebrew expresses the difference strongly, "The spirit of man that ascends, it belongeth to on high; but the spirit of the beast that descends, it belongeth to below, even to the earth." Their destinations and proper element differ utterly [Weiss]. <div eID="gen12482" type="x-p"/>

Inculcating a thankful enjoyment of God's gifts, and a cheerful discharge of man's duties, founded on fear of God; not as the sensualist (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>); not as the anxious money-seeker (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.23">Ec 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10-2Cor.5.17">5:10-17</reference>).<div eID="gen12483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his portion--</hi>in the present life. entries.content_plain: 22. (Compare Ec 3:12 ; 5:18 ). Inculcating a thankful enjoyment of God's gifts, and a cheerful discharge of man's duties, founded on fear of God; not as the sensualist ( Ec 11:9 ); not as the anxious money-seeker ( Ec 2:23 ; 5:10-17 ). his portion-- in the present life. If it were made his main portion, it would be "vanity" ( Ec 2:1 ; Lu 16:25 ). for who, &c.-- Our ignorance as to the future, which is God's "time" ( Ec 3:11 ), should lead us to use the present time in the best sense and leave the future to His infinite wisdom ( Mt 6:20 , 25, 31-34 ).
